mainEntity.name: How long does it take before a dental implant can bear load?

acceptedAnswer.text: The timeline varies depending on the loading protocol used and the individual patient's clinical situation. Conventional loading typically occurs after three to six months of healing, while early loading may occur between one and twelve weeks. In carefully selected cases, immediate loading on the same day as placement may be appropriate. Your dentist will advise on the most suitable timeline after assessing bone quality, implant stability, and your overall health. There is no single answer that applies to every patient.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat normally while waiting for my implant to integrate?

acceptedAnswer.text: During the healing phase, your dentist will provide guidance on dietary modifications. In the early weeks, softer foods are generally recommended to avoid placing unnecessary pressure on the implant site. As healing progresses and the implant gains stability, normal eating gradually resumes. Following these dietary guidelines supports the osseointegration process and helps protect the implant during a critical period of bone healing.

mainEntity.name: What happens if an implant is loaded too early?

acceptedAnswer.text: If an implant is subjected to functional forces before sufficient osseointegration has occurred, the mechanical stress can disrupt the developing bone-implant interface. This may result in implant micro-movement, which inhibits proper bone formation around the post. In some cases, this can compromise the long-term stability of the implant. This is why clinical assessment of implant stability and bone quality is essential before determining the loading protocol.

mainEntity.name: Does bone quality affect whether I am suitable for dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bone quality and volume are important factors in implant planning. Insufficient bone density or volume may mean that a bone grafting procedure is needed before or at the time of implant placement. Advances in bone regeneration techniques mean that many patients who were previously considered unsuitable may now have options available to them. A thorough clinical assessment, including dental imaging such as a CBCT scan, helps the dentist evaluate bone conditions accurately.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to feel pressure on an implant crown when biting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some patients notice a slight awareness of pressure when biting on a newly restored implant. A minor sensation of pressure can be normal as you adapt to the restoration. However, persistent pain, discomfort, or a feeling that the bite is uneven or uncomfortable should be mentioned to your dentist. These symptoms may indicate that the bite needs adjustment or that further assessment is warranted. Do not ignore ongoing discomfort around an implant.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my implant is integrating successfully?

acceptedAnswer.text: Successful osseointegration is assessed clinically by your dentist — it is not something that can be self-diagnosed at home. Signs that all is progressing well include the absence of pain, swelling, or movement around the implant. At review appointments, your dentist may use clinical tests or imaging to evaluate healing. If you experience increasing pain, swelling, or notice any changes around the implant site, contact your dental practice promptly for assessment.
